newsitem.title: FRANCE: Cost of French bank's lending spree rises.
newsitem.headline: Cost of French bank's lending spree rises.

text.p: France's new Socialist government was hit with bad news on Monday when a newspaper said losses from state-controlled bank Credit Lyonnais' disastrous lending spree could total nearly 170 billion francs ($30 billion).
The estimate brought home the costly consequences of the bank's expansion drive, carried out when the Socialists were previously in power in the 1980s and early 1990s.

Newspaper Le Parisien said the figure was in a report by the Etablissement Publique de Finance et de Restructuration (EPFR), a state body supervising the sale of bad assets removed from Credit Lyonnais' balance sheet under a 1995 government rescue.
In addition, the EPFR is seeking a 7.7 billion franc capital injection between now and year-end, it said.
Recapitalisation of the EPFR could make it harder for the government to cut France's deficit and qualify for European monetary union.
The paper said the loss estimate represented a cost of 6,000 francs for each French family.
The estimate has rocketed as the extent of the bank's misadventures has become known -- from just seven billion francs in 1993 to 50 billion in 1995 and 130 billion francs last March.

The EPFR calculated losses from selling the bank's assets, bought at the market's peak, at 102.8 billion francs. On top of that must be added 66 billion francs in carrying costs, bringing the total to nearly 170 billion francs, Le Parisien said.
The finance ministry said it had not yet received the 28-page report by the EPFR which calls for a full investigation of the causes of France's biggest banking horror story.
"The state will see what it has to do when it receives the report," said a finance ministry spokeswoman.
Investigators have launched 75 criminal suits in connection with the bank's troubles, 52 in France and 23 abroad.
Credit Lyonnais, which lost 21 billion francs between 1992 and 1994, has recovered strongly, helped by big state bailouts.
The previous conservative administration, turfed out by voters in May, had promised to privatise the bank but the Socialist government has halted all state sell-offs.
Conservative parliamentarian Charles de Courson -- who until the election was a government representative on the EPFR -- blamed the bank's problems on "disastrous management."
In an interview with Le Parisien, he singled out the bank's former chairman between 1998 and 1993, Jean-Yves Haberer, who he said had been politically protected.
When civil servants had sought to sound the alarm about the bank's risky investments, former Socialist finance minister Pierre Beregevoy told them to leave Haberer alone, he said.
He said the French Treasury and the Commission Bancaire, the industry watchdog, "had not done their work".
His allegations echoed those of a 1994 commission of inquiry which rapped the government and the Commission Bancaire but aimed its main guns at Haberer.

While stressing he could not be reproached for honesty, it said he ran a "quasi-monarchic regime" and presided over a "bulimia of investment" in which the bank build up expensive stakes in 1,500 firms, lent recklessly to developers and dished out huge sums to buy other European banks.
Haberer has said the bank was under political pressure from the previous Socialist government to make its loans and support French business.
($ = 5.836 French Francs)
